edges.effect_quant: The aggregate literature leans modestly protective, but not every strain works. A 2012 meta-analysis found a pooled RR of 0.79 for atopic dermatitis after probiotics given in pregnancy or early life, while one large trial of Lactobacillus rhamnosus HN001 reported a hazard ratio of 0.51 for eczema at 2 years, yet another placebo-controlled Lactobacillus GG trial found no reduction with a relative risk of 0.96.
edges.population: infants and high-risk mother-infant pairs receiving probiotic supplementation during pregnancy, early infancy, or both
edges.mechanism: Early probiotic exposure may help shape gut colonization and immune tolerance during a period when allergic sensitization pathways are still plastic, but the effect appears to depend heavily on strain, timing, and whether the mother, infant, or both receive the intervention.
edges.summary: This edge is best read as mixed but somewhat favorable. Meta-analyses and some strain-specific randomized trials suggest that early-life probiotics can modestly lower eczema risk by age 2, yet other well-run trials have been neutral, which argues against treating probiotics as a uniform eczema-prevention tool.
edges.caveats: The literature is highly strain-specific and mixes maternal, infant, and combined supplementation strategies. Positive results with one Lactobacillus strain do not guarantee that another probiotic product will reproduce the same atopic-dermatitis benefit.
